title: Higher-Dimensional Polytopes Glossary
description: Concepts covering 4D and higher polytopes, spherical and hyperbolic tilings, high-dimensional lattices, and the binary icosahedral group, serving as comparison spaces for flat-space constructions.

5-cell.summary: The simplest regular 4-polytope, with 5 tetrahedral cells; the 4D analogue of the tetrahedron.
5-cell.definition: The **4D simplex**: the simplest 4-polytope, with 5 tetrahedral cells, 10 triangular faces, 10 edges, and 5 vertices. Self-dual. Analogue of the tetrahedron. Its Schläfli symbol is $\{3, 3, 3\}$ and its symmetry group has order 120.

examples.title: Euler characteristic
examples.body: The 5-cell has 5 vertices, 10 edges, 10 triangular faces, and 5 tetrahedral cells. Euler characteristic: 5 - 10 + 10 - 5 = 0, consistent with a 4D polytope.

examples.title: Self-duality
examples.body: The dual of the 5-cell is another 5-cell. Swapping vertices and cells, and edges and faces, yields an isomorphic polytope.

formulas.description: Schläfli symbol of the 5-cell: tetrahedral cells with 3 meeting at each edge.

8-cell.summary: The 4D analogue of the cube, with 8 cubic cells; also known as the tesseract.
8-cell.definition: The **4D analogue of the cube**: 8 cubic cells, 24 square faces, 32 edges, 16 vertices. Often referred to as the **tesseract** in popular literature. Its Schläfli symbol is $\{4, 3, 3\}$, its symmetry group has order 384, and it forms the unit cell of $\mathbb{Z}^4$.

examples.title: Unit cell of Z^4
examples.body: The 8-cell tiles 4-dimensional Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^4$ by translation, forming the hypercubic lattice $\mathbb{Z}^4$. Each vertex has integer coordinates.

examples.title: Unfolding
examples.body: Just as a cube unfolds into a cross of 6 squares, the tesseract unfolds into a cross of 8 cubes in 3D space.

formulas.description: Schläfli symbol of the 8-cell: cubic cells with 3 meeting at each edge.

16-cell.summary: The 4D analogue of the octahedron, with 16 tetrahedral cells; dual to the 8-cell.
16-cell.definition: The **4D analogue of the octahedron**: 16 tetrahedral cells, 32 triangular faces, 24 edges, 8 vertices. Its Schläfli symbol is $\{3, 3, 4\}$, its symmetry group has order 384, and it is dual to the 8-cell.

examples.title: Duality with the 8-cell
examples.body: The 16-cell is the dual of the 8-cell: its 8 vertices correspond to the 8 cells of the tesseract, and its 16 cells correspond to the 16 vertices of the tesseract.

formulas.description: Schläfli symbol of the 16-cell: tetrahedral cells with 4 meeting at each edge.

24-cell.summary: A uniquely 4D regular polytope with no 3D Platonic analogue, with 24 octahedral cells; self-dual and tiles R^4.
24-cell.definition: A **uniquely 4D polytope** with no Platonic analogue in 3D. It has 24 octahedral cells, 96 triangular faces, 96 edges, and 24 vertices. Its Schläfli symbol is $\{3, 4, 3\}$, its symmetry group has order 1152, it is **self-dual**, and it tiles $\mathbb{R}^4$.

examples.title: Self-duality
examples.body: The dual of the 24-cell is another 24-cell. This is one of only three regular polytopes (across all dimensions) that are self-dual: the simplex family, the 24-cell, and the square.

examples.title: Tiling R^4
examples.body: The 24-cell tiles 4-dimensional Euclidean space by translation and rotation, forming the unique regular honeycomb $\{3,4,3,3\}$ in 4D.

formulas.description: Schläfli symbol of the 24-cell: octahedral cells with 3 meeting at each edge.

120-cell.summary: The 4D analogue of the dodecahedron, with 120 dodecahedral cells; tiles the 3-sphere S^3.
120-cell.definition: The **4D analogue of the dodecahedron**: 120 dodecahedral cells, 720 pentagonal faces, 1200 edges, and 600 vertices. Its Schläfli symbol is $\{5, 3, 3\}$. It **tiles the 3-sphere $S^3$**. Its symmetry group has order $14400$ and is related to the **binary icosahedral group $2I$**. Dual to the 600-cell.

examples.title: Tiling S^3
examples.body: The 120-cell provides a regular cell decomposition of the 3-sphere $S^3$, with exactly 120 dodecahedral cells fitting together without gap or overlap. This is the 4D analogue of the dodecahedron tiling $S^2$.

examples.title: Duality with the 600-cell
examples.body: The dual of the 120-cell is the 600-cell: the 600 vertices of the 120-cell correspond to the 600 cells of the 600-cell, and vice versa.

formulas.description: Schläfli symbol of the 120-cell: dodecahedral cells with 3 meeting at each edge.
Order of the symmetry group of the 120-cell, related to the binary icosahedral group.

600-cell.summary: The 4D analogue of the icosahedron, with 600 tetrahedral cells; dual to the 120-cell, its vertices are the 120 icosian quaternions.
600-cell.definition: The **4D analogue of the icosahedron**: 600 tetrahedral cells, 1200 triangular faces, 720 edges, and 120 vertices. Its Schläfli symbol is $\{3, 3, 5\}$. **Dual to the 120-cell**. Its 120 vertices form the **icosian quaternions** of the binary icosahedral group $2I$.

examples.title: Vertices as icosians
examples.body: The 120 vertices of the 600-cell, when viewed as unit quaternions, are precisely the 120 elements of the binary icosahedral group $2I$. These are the icosian quaternions with coefficients in $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5})$.

examples.title: Duality with the 120-cell
examples.body: The dual of the 600-cell is the 120-cell. The 120 vertices of the 600-cell correspond to the 120 cells of the 120-cell.

formulas.description: Schläfli symbol of the 600-cell: tetrahedral cells with 5 meeting at each edge.

spherical-tiling.summary: A tiling of a sphere S^n by regular polygons or polyhedra, characterized by positive curvature and angular surplus.
spherical-tiling.definition:
A **tiling of a sphere $S^n$**. Examples include the dodecahedron tiling $S^2$ (its 12 pentagonal faces are spherical pentagons after central projection) and the 120-cell tiling $S^3$. Each Platonic solid tiles $S^2$ when projected.

Spherical tilings have **positive curvature**: angles sum to **more** than the flat value. This angular surplus is precisely the curvature integral over each face (Gauss–Bonnet). For the dodecahedron viewed as a tiling of $S^2$, exactly **3 pentagons** meet at each vertex.

examples.title: Dodecahedron on S^2
examples.body: The dodecahedron tiles $S^2$ with 12 spherical pentagonal faces. Exactly 3 pentagons meet at each vertex, and the angular surplus at each vertex is $360° - 3 \times 108° = -\,(-36°) = 36°$ (positive surplus relative to flat space).

examples.title: 120-cell on S^3
examples.body: The 120-cell tiles $S^3$ with 120 dodecahedral cells. The positive curvature of $S^3$ absorbs the angular deficit that would prevent a flat tiling by dodecahedra.

examples.title: Platonic solids as spherical tilings
examples.body: All five Platonic solids tile $S^2$ via central projection: tetrahedron $\{3,3\}$, cube $\{4,3\}$, octahedron $\{3,4\}$, dodecahedron $\{5,3\}$, icosahedron $\{3,5\}$.

formulas.description: Condition for a Schläfli symbol {p,q} to correspond to a spherical tiling (positive curvature). Satisfied by the five Platonic solids.

variables.p: Number of sides of each polygonal face
variables.q: Number of faces meeting at each vertex

hyperbolic-tiling.summary: A tiling of the hyperbolic plane H^2 or higher hyperbolic space, supporting configurations impossible in flat or spherical space.
hyperbolic-tiling.definition:
A **tiling of the hyperbolic plane** $\mathbb{H}^2$ (or higher-dimensional hyperbolic space). Supports **otherwise-forbidden configurations** such as 4 or more pentagons at each vertex. Hyperbolic tilings have **negative curvature**: the angular deficit becomes an angular surplus (more than $2\pi$ would fit around a vertex), which the curvature absorbs.

Examples:
- **{5, 4}** tiling: 4 pentagons at each vertex (impossible in flat space).
- **{5, 5}**, **{5, 6}**, etc.: arbitrarily many pentagons at each vertex.
- **{7, 3}**, **{8, 3}**, etc.: regular tilings by polygons that cannot tile $\mathbb{R}^2$.

examples.title: {5, 4} tiling
examples.body: In the hyperbolic plane, 4 regular pentagons can meet at each vertex. The interior angle of a hyperbolic regular pentagon can be made equal to $90°$, so $4 \times 90° = 360°$ fits exactly. This is impossible in Euclidean space where a regular pentagon has interior angles of $108°$.

examples.title: {7, 3} tiling
examples.body: Three regular heptagons meet at each vertex in the hyperbolic plane. The Fano plane and certain Riemann surfaces are related to this tiling.

formulas.description: Condition for a Schläfli symbol {p,q} to correspond to a hyperbolic tiling (negative curvature). Satisfied by infinitely many pairs (p,q).

variables.p: Number of sides of each polygonal face
variables.q: Number of faces meeting at each vertex

schlafli-symbol.summary: A compact notation {p, q} or {p, q, r} classifying regular tilings and polytopes by their face type and vertex configuration.
schlafli-symbol.definition:
A compact notation indicating the structure of a regular tiling or polytope:
- $\{p, q\}$: a tiling by regular $p$-gons with $q$ of them meeting at each vertex (2D tiling or 3D polytope boundary).
- $\{p, q, r\}$: a regular 4-polytope with cells $\{p, q\}$ and $r$ cells meeting at each edge.

The geometry is determined by the curvature condition:
- **Flat (Euclidean)**: $(p-2)(q-2) = 4$. Solutions: $\{3,6\}, \{4,4\}, \{6,3\}$.
- **Spherical**: $(p-2)(q-2) < 4$. (The five Platonic solids.)
- **Hyperbolic**: $(p-2)(q-2) > 4$. (Infinitely many examples.)

examples.title: Pentagon tilings
examples.body: For pentagons ($p=5$): $\{5,3\}$ is the dodecahedron (spherical, angular sum $324° < 360°$); $\{5,4\}$ is hyperbolic (angular sum $432° > 360°$); no flat $\{5,q\}$ exists.

examples.title: Flat tilings
examples.body: The three flat tilings are $\{3,6\}$ (triangular), $\{4,4\}$ (square), and $\{6,3\}$ (hexagonal), all satisfying $(p-2)(q-2)=4$.

formulas.description: Flatness condition for a regular tiling {p,q}.

variables.p: Number of sides of each face
variables.q: Number of faces at each vertex

formulas.description: Spherical (positive curvature) condition for a regular tiling {p,q}.
Hyperbolic (negative curvature) condition for a regular tiling {p,q}.

hypercubic-lattice.summary: The integer lattice Z^n in R^n, whose Voronoi cell is the unit hypercube; serves as the source space for cut-and-project quasicrystal constructions.
hypercubic-lattice.definition:
The **integer lattice in $\mathbb{R}^n$**: the set of all points with integer coordinates. The Voronoi cell of $\mathbb{Z}^n$ is the unit hypercube $[0,1]^n$. Its symmetry group includes the **hyperoctahedral group** of order $2^n n!$.

Key instances in the project:
- $\mathbb{Z}^4$: target of 4D quasicrystal projections.
- $\mathbb{Z}^5$: cut-and-project source of the Penrose tiling.
- $\mathbb{Z}^6$: cut-and-project source of the AKN tiling (icosahedral quasicrystal).

examples.title: Z^5 and the Penrose tiling
examples.body: The Penrose tiling is obtained by projecting a 2D slice of $\mathbb{Z}^5$ onto a plane oriented at an irrational angle with respect to the lattice axes. The five basis vectors of $\mathbb{Z}^5$ project to the five directions of pentagonal symmetry.

examples.title: Z^6 and the icosahedral quasicrystal
examples.body: The 3D icosahedral quasicrystal (AKN tiling) is obtained by projecting a 3D slice of $\mathbb{Z}^6$ onto a 3D subspace with icosahedral symmetry.

examples.title: Hyperoctahedral symmetry
examples.body: The symmetry group of $\mathbb{Z}^n$ is the hyperoctahedral group $B_n$ of order $2^n n!$, generated by permutations and sign changes of coordinates.

formulas.description: Definition of the integer lattice in n dimensions.
Order of the symmetry group of the hypercubic lattice Z^n.

binary-icosahedral-group.summary: The double cover of the icosahedral group I in SU(2), of order 120; realized as the 120 icosian unit quaternions forming the vertices of the 600-cell.
binary-icosahedral-group.definition:
The **double cover of the icosahedral group $I$** in $SU(2)$:
$$2I = \text{Spin}(3)\text{-lift of } I \subset SO(3)$$
Order $|2I| = 2 \times 60 = 120$.

The 120 elements of $2I$ can be written as **unit quaternions with coefficients in $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5})$** — the so-called **icosians**. They include:
- 8 elements $\{\pm 1, \pm i, \pm j, \pm k\}$.
- 16 elements $\frac{1}{2}(\pm 1 \pm i \pm j \pm k)$.
- 96 elements obtained from $\frac{1}{2}(0, \pm 1, \pm \phi^{-1}, \pm \phi)$ by even cyclic permutations and sign changes.

Roles in the project:
- **Vertices of the 600-cell** are the 120 icosians.
- $2I$ acts on the 120-cell and 600-cell.
- Provides the algebraic structure for 3D pentagonal/icosahedral tilings.
- Encodes **spinor doubling**: the holonomy of certain loops in pentagon-related multi-sheeted covers lifts to $2I$ via $SU(2) \to SO(3)$.

examples.title: Icosians as unit quaternions
examples.body: The 120 icosians are unit quaternions $q = a + bi + cj + dk$ where $a, b, c, d \in \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5})$ and $|q|=1$. They form a group under quaternion multiplication isomorphic to $2I$.

examples.title: Spinor doubling
examples.body: The covering map $SU(2) \to SO(3)$ sends $2I$ onto the icosahedral group $I \cong A_5$ of order 60. A loop in $SO(3)$ that returns to the identity may lift to a path in $SU(2)$ ending at $-1$, encoding the spinor (half-turn) nature of the double cover.

examples.title: 600-cell vertices
examples.body: The 120 vertices of the 600-cell, embedded in $\mathbb{R}^4 \cong \mathbb{H}$, are precisely the 120 icosian quaternions. Left and right multiplication by elements of $2I$ generate the full symmetry group of the 600-cell.

formulas.description: Order of the binary icosahedral group, twice the order of the icosahedral group I ≅ A_5.
Short exact sequence expressing 2I as a central extension of the icosahedral group I by Z/2.
The golden ratio, appearing in the quaternion coordinates of the icosians.

dimensional-hierarchy.summary: The propagation of the pentagon's angular obstruction across dimensions, resolved by spherical geometry, hyperbolic geometry, or multi-sheeted flat covers.
dimensional-hierarchy.definition:
The pentagon's angular obstruction (36° deficit per vertex) propagates upward through dimensions:

- **2D**: Pentagon → multi-sheeted plane (fiber: $\mathbb{Z}/10$).
- **3D**: Dodecahedron → multi-sheeted $\mathbb{R}^3$ (fiber: subgroup of $I$, possibly $2I$).
- **4D**: 120-cell tiles $S^3$ exactly (no deficit because $S^3$ supplies curvature).

Three resolutions of pentagonal frustration exist:
1. **Spherical**: dodecahedron on $S^2$, 120-cell on $S^3$ — positive curvature absorbs deficit.
2. **Hyperbolic**: $\{5, q\}$ for $q \geq 4$ — negative curvature absorbs surplus.
3. **Multi-sheeted flat**: pentagon expansion family on multi-sheeted $\mathbb{R}^2$ — covering space absorbs deficit as **monodromy**.

The project focuses on the third route, but the other two provide essential context and comparison.

examples.title: 2D: multi-sheeted plane
examples.body: A regular pentagon has an interior angle of 108°. Three pentagons at a vertex give 324°, leaving a 36° deficit. In the multi-sheeted construction, this deficit is absorbed by the monodromy of the covering map, with fiber group Z/10.

examples.title: 4D: exact tiling of S^3
examples.body: The 120-cell tiles $S^3$ exactly because the positive curvature of $S^3$ provides precisely the angular surplus needed to compensate the 36° deficit per vertex of the dodecahedral cells.

formulas.description: The angular deficit at each vertex when three regular pentagons meet in flat space.
